notes.52v.9c: '.í. born' (52v.4d) pairs the numeral 'one' with what looks like a plural noun; perhaps 'two young' was meant, and 52v.30 speaks of the hind's young in the plural. The numerals .í., .xí. and .ííí. are read with the edition's values, 2, 12 and 4: the scribe's final long i can count as two.
notes.125r.9: Scribal doublings: 'drendrengr' (125r.4b) for drengr 'warrior', and 'lœprlœypr' (125r.5b) for hleypr 'leaps'. 'sigis froð kiallara' (125v.21) is read as 'Sigfrod's cellar'; the form of the name is uncertain.
notes.55r.9a: 'hvertrhvert' (55r.11a) is a scribal doubling of hvert 'whither'.
notes.109r.2c: 'hæfdihæfndi' in the heading (387.h) is a scribal doubling of hefndi 'avenged'.
notes.111v.10: Sigurd Svein ('the lad') is Sigurd's name in this saga.
notes.112v.3b: gauðgandr is obscure; it seems to name her sorcery (gandr is a magic staff or spirit). 'We call it' introduces the writer's explanation of what she did. 'or' before 'biorno' (line 12) is read as 'and'.
notes.276.h: Line 1 is a chapter heading, with 'brothers' written twice in two spellings. The dead king is named jrungr (Irung) here although his eldest son is Gunnar; perhaps a slip for Gunnar's father. hallzi (line 5) is unclear; taken as 'holder'.
notes.110v.10b: Line 2 is a chapter heading. Line 1 writes 'þæssir' and 'þæssar' side by side; riðir is taken as hríðir, 'times', i.e. 'for this while'.
notes.124r.9b: Troia here is Hogni's home in this saga, not ancient Troy.

then

it has long benefited
since, because he held and built
his kingdom.
Of Sigurd the boy.
This same glass vessel drifts down
the river to the sea, and that is not very far. And it is
now ebb tide. Now there drifts
the vessel onto a sandbank. Now
the sea falls away, so that it is all dry where
the vessel lies.
Now the boy has grown somewhat, and when the vessel knocks
against the sandbank, then
it breaks apart, and the child cries.
Now a hind came there and takes
the child in her mouth
and carries it home to her lair. There she had two young.
There she lays
the boy down and lets the boy suck
from her, and there she rears him as
her own young. And he is
there with the hind twelve months. Now he is as strong
and big as other children four winters old.
Of Mimir and Regin.
A man was called Mimir. He is a smith
so famous and so skilful that hardly
was there any
equal to him in that craft. He has many lads with him
who serve him. He has a wife, and in the nine
winters since he
married her they have not been able
to have a child, and that grieves him much. He
has
a brother who was called Regin. He was formidable
in his own right, and of all
men the worst, and he was also
repaid for that, in that he got such great
spells and sorcery
that he turned into a serpent. And now it came about that he
was
of all serpents the greatest and worst. And now he means to kill every
man
except that he is good to his brother. And
now he is the strongest of all, and now
no man knows
his lair except his brother Mimir.
Of Mimir and Sigurd the boy.
Now it happens one day that Mimir means
to go into the forest and burn charcoal, and
he means to be there
three days. And when he comes into the forest, they make
big fires. And when he is standing by the fire all
alone, then there comes
up to him a boy. He was
handsome, and runs to him. He asks what
kind of boy he
might be. But the boy cannot speak. But still Mimir takes
him to
himself and sets him on his knee and lays clothes over
him, because he had
no clothes before. And then there comes
a hind running there, and goes up to the knees
of Mimir
and licks the face and head of the child all over. And from that
Mimir thinks he knows that the hind must have fostered
the child, and for that reason he will
not destroy the hind.
And he takes the boy and keeps him, and takes [him] home
with
him, and now means to raise him as his son, and gives
[him] a name, and calls [him]
Sigfrod. Now that boy grows up there
until he is nine winters old, and
he is now
so big and strong that no man saw his equal.
He is so
hard to deal with that he beats and knocks about
Mimir's lads, so that it hardly seems
bearable to be near him.
Of Sigurd and Ekkihard.
One lad is called Ekkihard.

and now he wants

if he will not kill Mimir, then

Sigurd kills Mimir, his foster-father.
Now Ekkihard is outside and sees where
Sigurd is going, and goes to his master and said: Yes,
lord, now there comes
and they are the best of all weapons. And a horse I will give
you, which is called
Grani; it is in Brynhild's stud. And a

is the best of all swords. Now
Brynhild says: If you
do not know how to tell me, then I can tell you
that you are Sigurd, son of King Sigmund and of Sisibe.
And you shall be welcome here
with us. But where have you
Of King Gunnar and his brothers.
But when King Irung passes away, then
his son Gunnar takes,
the eldest, over the kingdom, and
so he becomes its holder. King Thidrek has true
his life, as long as he wishes.
The marriage of Sigurd and Gunnar.
Now King Thidrek and all his
men have proved themselves
in this, that no man in the world
made which has since become very famous: that Sigurd
Svein shall go
and marry Grimhild, the sister of Gunnar
the king and of Hogni, and take with her half
of King Gunnar's kingdom. And now there is made ready
she is beyond all other women
in intelligence and courtliness and all wisdom, and in nobility of spirit
and high ambition. And she is called Brynhild. She rules
over the stronghold which is called Segard. This woman
you should take as your wife, and in this I can be
wept again, anew, at her death.

Here begins the saga of the Niflungs, and of the dealings between Young Sigurd and Hogni and King Gunnar, and of the battle in Susat, and how Grimhild avenged her dishonour, which was done to her without cause in the beginning; and here begin the chapters.
At this time in the land of the Niflungs, in
that city
which is called Verniza, there rules Gunnar,
the king, and with him his
brother Hogni and the
men's.
Of Grimhild and Brynhild.
Now it happens one time that Queen
Brynhild goes
into her hall, and there before her sits
Grimhild, King Gunnar's sister,
and when Brynhild
comes to her seat, she spoke to Grimhild:
not at home now for this while.
Of Hogni and Sigurd Svein.
A few days later, in the evening, there comes
home Sigurd Svein with his
men, and when
has talked with
Queen Brynhild a long while, and
in their private talk it is this, that Brynhild asks
Hogni to arrange it so that Sigurd
Svein shall not come home

like the others. And then Hogni stands up
when

But Gernoz is certainly dead. And now she goes

and thrusts the firebrand into the mouth

dies
Gislher. Now King Thidrek of Bern sees what
Grimhild is doing, and spoke
to King Attila:
See how the devil Grimhild, your wife, torments
her brothers,
good warriors, and how many a man
has lost his life for her sake,
and how
many good men she has destroyed, Huns
and Amelungs and
Niflungs; and in just the same way
she would bring you to your death, and me, if it
were possible
for her. Then King Attila said: Truly she is a devil.
Kill her.
And that would have been a good deed, if you
had done it nights ago.
Then many a
splendid warrior would be whole who now is dead. Now
King Thidrek leaps
at Grimhild and hews
her asunder at the middle. Now King Thidrek goes
to
Hogni and asks whether he can be healed.
Hogni says that he will
live some
days, but there is no hope that he will not die of
these
wounds. Now King Thidrek has [men] carry
Hogni home into his hall and bind
his wounds. Herrad
was the name of a kinswoman of King Thidrek. He gets her
to bind
his wounds. And in the evening Hogni says to
King Thidrek that he should get him
a woman, and says
that he wants to sleep with [her] in the night. And so does
Thidrek.
And in the morning Hogni says to this
woman: Now it may be, when from now
some
time has passed, that you will have a son by me, and
that
boy shall be called Aldrian. And here are keys which you shall
keep
and give to that boy when he is grown.
These keys fit Sigfrod's cellar,
in which is
stored the Niflungs' treasure. And after this Hogni dies.
And now
the life of the Niflungs is ended, and so of all the
most powerful men in the land of the
Huns, except King Attila
married in Niflungaland. Here one may now hear
the account of German men, how these
events went,
certain of whom were born
in Susat, where these happenings
took place, and
for many a day have seen the places still unchanged,
the same as when the events took place: where Hogni fell, or Irung
was
